# NOT A FIXTURE. A fixture fails when behaviour REGRESSES. This fails BOTH
# ways: when a port is repaired to agree with another, the row still
# claims they differ, so the suite goes red and names the row to delete. A
# divergence recorded as a passing test of current behaviour survives its
# own repair, with nothing red — which is how the 2026-08 audit found 29

# --- Astral characters: the column UNIT, and it is PERMANENT --------------
# TypeScript counts UTF-16 code units, so an astral character advances the
# column by TWO; Go counts runes, so it advances by one. Forced by the scan
# unit — TS scans UTF-16 code units, Go scans UTF-8 bytes — and recorded in
# parser/DIVERGENCE.md, "Column positions for astral characters". Nothing
# below the BMP disagrees, which is what the two deleted rows used to show.
# WHAT WAS HERE, AND WHY IT IS NOT. Four rows recorded audit item P5: Go
# adding one column per extra BYTE, so a two-byte 'é' cost two columns and
# a four-byte emoji four. The header said "these rows go red on adoption,
# which is the signal to delete them", and on adoption they did exactly
# that — this file is not a fixture, it fails when a port is REPAIRED as
# well as when one regresses. The repair was #51 (go/strmatcher.go), which
# merged while this register was still in flight on another branch.
#   ["é" 1]   go 1:6 -> 1:5, now equal to ts     CLOSED, deleted
#   ["€" 1]   go 1:7 -> 1:5, now equal to ts     CLOSED, deleted

# closed: go 1:8 -> 1:5 and 1:12 -> 1:9, each still one short of the TS
# column because of the surrogate pair. They are re-attributed rather than
# deleted — same rows, different reason, and the reason is now the argued
# and permanent one instead of a repairable defect.
# MEASURED against the SIBLING CHECKOUTS, which is what CI tests: the

input: # --- A string escape where the three ports are not unanimous -------------
# `\u12g4` is a lax hexadecimal scan. The canonical `isHexadecimal`
# accepts every ASCII letter and `parseInt` then reads the longest hex
# PREFIX, so TypeScript answers U+0012 and swallows the rest; the Rust port
# reproduces it deliberately, since TypeScript is canonical. Go's scan is
# strict and rejects. GO IS THE REPAIR TARGET, not the defect: `"\u12g4"`
# is invalid TOML -- the format requires exactly four hexadecimal digits --
# so the port that rejects it is the one a reader would call right, and the
# two that move are TypeScript and Rust. That is what makes this a real
# question rather than a sweep.
# A SECOND escape belongs in this class and cannot be written down here.
# `a = "\ud801"` is a lone surrogate: a JavaScript string keeps it, and a
# Rust `char` and a Go rune are Unicode SCALAR values, so both fold it to
# U+FFFD. The cell vocabulary is JSON, and the JSON decoders in two of the
# three halves fold a lone surrogate to U+FFFD while reading the `ts` cell
# itself, so all three cells compare equal and the row asserts nothing.
# That difference is permanent, comes from the engine and is recorded in
# parser/DIVERGENCE.md and in rs/README.md.
# MEASURED 2026-09-22 in all three ports.

why: lax hexadecimal scan: Go is right, TS and Rust move

input: # All three ports refuse a redefined key with toml_key_conflict (the shared

# Rust point at the key being redefined, `a` in `[a]` on line 2. TypeScript
# answers 1:1: the plugin raises on `ctx.t0`, and its engine has moved the
# matched tokens into the rewind history and emptied the slot by the time an
# alternate's action runs (tabnas/parser ts/src/rules.ts, the consumed-token
# shift before `alt.a`), so the error is built from the NOTOKEN sentinel.
# TYPESCRIPT IS THE REPAIR TARGET: the two ports that name the line the
# reader has to look at are right, and the repair is in ts/src/toml.ts
# (raise on the matched key token, `r.o0`) or in the engine. Not a code
# divergence, so no spec row is affected.
# MEASURED 2026-10-02 in all three ports.
